catalog_citation: Rutter, Owen. 1929. The Pagans of North Borneo. London: Hutchinson & Co. Appendix A: Comparative Vocabulary (thirteen Murut and Dusun dialects, incl. a Kuijau column), pp. 262-275; introductory note p. 262.
catalog_locator: p. 262, Appendix A (Comparative Vocabulary, pp. 262-275; Appendix B begins p. 276), introductory note, first paragraph (archive.org item pagansofnorthbor0000owen, leaf 392). Marked non-penult forms in the Kuijau row checked on p. 266, p. 271 and p. 272; start of Appendix B checked on p. 276.
catalog_quote: I compiled these vocabularies, which contain the words (186) which Sir James Frazer recommends for collection, during the years I was in the North Borneo Civil Service. They cover thirteen pagan dialects and each was made with the assistance of a native of the group in question and checked whenever possible; my informants were rather above the average pagan intelligence; all could speak, and most of them write, Malay. The spelling is phonetic, the letter sounds as in Malay and the accentuation, as in Malay, is on the penultimate syllable unless otherwise shown. The final ‘ k ’ is almost mute.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the 186-item wordlists (which include a Kuijau column), accent is on the penultimate syllable of the word, 'as in Malay', with any deviation to be marked on the individual entry; no accent marks are visible on the Kuijau entries in the scanned layer.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the escape clause 'unless otherwise shown'; no explicit exceptions are discussed, and the scanned shows no marked forms in the Kuijau column (accent marks may not survive scanned).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in a comparative wordlist; a single orthographic convention applied to all 13 dialects (Marudu, Tempasuk, Tuaran, Kiau, Putatan, Papar, Tambunan Dusun, Kuijau, Keningau/Peluan/Tenom/Rundum Murut, Tengara). Author admits 'no more than a smattering of Dusun and Murut'. Weak, second-tier evidence; no phonological description of Kuijau exists (Spitzack 1984: 'no serious linguistic description has ever been attempted').
new_statements.identity_note: Rutter's 'Kuijau' column (Keningau Plain, 1920s) is the same group Glottolog calls Kuijau [kuij1237]; Lobel 2013 spells it Kujau, Rutter 1922 Kwijau, Prentice 1970 'Menindaq'/'Minansut'. Smith 1984 split off 'Apin-Apin Kuijau' as Murutic; Rutter's list is not that variety. The stress note is a blanket convention stated once for all thirteen Murut and Dusun vocabularies in the appendix, not a Kuijau-specific observation.

sources.note: Nothing. Lexicostatistics, dialect and intelligibility survey only; sec. 0.4 states no serious linguistic description of Kuijau has ever been attempted and lists Rutter 1929, Prentice 1970 and Cohen 1981 wordlists. The entire PL-C78 volume (incl. Spitzack's Murutic family chapter and Smith's classification) has zero occurrences of 'stress' or 'accent'.
